reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone / standard orthopaedic oncology texts
clinicalPearls: A locally aggressive benign tumour that classically arises in the epiphysis and extends to the subchondral bone of long bones in skeletally mature young adults
Common sites are around the knee (distal femur and proximal tibia) and the distal radius, typically in patients aged twenty to forty
Presents with progressive pain, swelling and reduced joint movement, and sometimes with a pathological fracture
Radiographs show an eccentric, expansile, purely lytic epiphyseal lesion abutting the articular surface, often described as having a soap-bubble appearance
The characteristic neoplastic mononuclear stromal cells overexpress RANKL, recruiting the numerous osteoclast-like giant cells that drive the osteolysis
Although benign, it is locally aggressive with a notable recurrence rate, and a small proportion develop benign pulmonary implants or, rarely, malignant transformation
Management is chiefly surgical (curettage with adjuvants or wider resection), with RANKL-directed therapy such as denosumab used for unresectable, recurrent or selected cases
reference.pathophysiology: Giant cell tumour of bone is composed of neoplastic mononuclear stromal cells together with reactive macrophages and abundant osteoclast-like multinucleated giant cells. The neoplastic stromal cells, which frequently carry a characteristic H3F3A histone gene mutation, secrete receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL), which recruits and activates the giant cells and drives extensive bone resorption. This produces the expansile, purely lytic epiphyseal lesion that reaches the subchondral bone. The RANKL pathway is the rationale for denosumab therapy. Despite its benign classification the tumour behaves in a locally aggressive manner and can seed benign, slowly growing pulmonary implants.
additionalDifferentials: Metastasis or plasmacytoma in older patients
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs showing an eccentric expansile lytic epiphyseal lesion abutting the joint
CT to assess cortical integrity and matrix
MRI to define soft-tissue extension and joint involvement
Chest imaging to detect pulmonary implants
Biopsy with histopathology and, where available, testing for the H3F3A mutation
Serum calcium and parathyroid hormone to exclude a brown tumour
redFlags: Rapid growth, marked cortical destruction or a soft-tissue mass suggesting malignant transformation or giant-cell-rich osteosarcoma
Pulmonary nodules indicating benign implants or, rarely, metastasis
reference.prognosis: The tumour is benign but locally aggressive, with recurrence after intralesional surgery an important concern; wider resection lowers recurrence at the cost of function. A minority develop pulmonary implants, and malignant transformation, although rare, worsens the outlook considerably.
pitfalls: Assuming a benign label means an indolent course and underestimating local aggressiveness and recurrence
Missing giant-cell-rich osteosarcoma or a brown tumour of hyperparathyroidism in the differential
Neglecting chest imaging for pulmonary implants
Inadequate intralesional curettage without adjuvant treatment leading to high recurrence
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone
management: Treat most lesions with intralesional curettage, a local adjuvant such as phenol or cryotherapy with high-speed burring, and defect filling with bone cement or graft
Undertake wider en-bloc resection and reconstruction for extensive, expendable-site, or recurrent disease
Use the RANKL inhibitor denosumab for unresectable, axial or sacral tumours, to downstage before surgery, and for pulmonary implants
Stabilise or reconstruct pathological fractures as part of surgical planning
Survey with local imaging for recurrence and chest imaging for pulmonary implants
Confirm the diagnosis with biopsy and H3F3A mutation testing before definitive treatment
Manage within an orthopaedic oncology multidisciplinary team
